name: Fortran
title: Fortran (2023)

type.text: **Typing is static but implicit typing is the default**: Without `implicit none`, a name beginning with I–N is an `integer` and every other name is a `real`, so a misspelled variable becomes a new one rather than an error
**There are no sum types**: An alternative is encoded as an integer tag beside the payload fields, and `select case` or `select type` must decode it, so nothing checks that the right branch was taken

**There are no generics, and a generic interface overloads a name instead**: An `interface` block binds one name to several specific procedures and the compiler resolves the call by argument type, which is overloading without a type parameter

**Operator and assignment overloading is expressible**: `interface operator(+)` and `interface assignment(=)` redefine `+` and `=` for a derived type, so the work behind an operator is invisible at the call site
**A module is a namespace with a selective import**: `use mymodule, only: a, b` brings in two names and nothing else, so no flat global namespace is imposed

**`class(t)` and `select type` give checked run-time polymorphism**: A polymorphic dummy argument dispatches on the dynamic type of the actual argument, and `select type` narrows it in a checked branch

construction.text: **Global mutable state is the default storage class**: A module variable and a `common` block are shared by every procedure that names them, and a variable marked `save` keeps its value between calls
**There is no immutability by default**: Only a `parameter` names a constant, and a module variable is writable by any user unless it carries the Fortran 2003 `protected` attribute

**A structure constructor validates nothing**: `t(a, b)` fills the components in order or by keyword, and no invariant can be stated at the type, so a valid object exists only because the caller made it valid
**A `pure` procedure states the absence of side effects**: It may not write a global, an `intent(in)` argument, or a `save`d variable, and the compiler enforces the rule

**`intent(in)`, `intent(out)`, and `intent(inout)` state the direction of an argument**: The declaration says whether a routine reads, writes, or does both, and the compiler checks it at the call site
**`elemental` states an elementwise operation**: An `elemental` procedure applies to each element of an array, so a scalar definition composes with array construction without a written loop

memory.text: **`allocate` and `deallocate` are written by hand for a `pointer`**: The language tracks no owner and no bound, so a pointer target is freed by an explicit statement and a missing one leaks
**There is no ownership model**: A `pointer` may alias a `target`, dangle after `deallocate`, or be freed twice, and the compiler does not see the aliasing

**Release tied to scope is partial**: An allocatable local and a derived-type component with a `final` procedure are released at scope exit, but a `pointer` is not, so the rule differs by variable kind
**An allocation failure must be tested**: `allocate(a(n), stat=ierr)` returns a code the program has to check, and without `stat=` a failure aborts the program
**`move_alloc` transfers an allocation without a copy**: `call move_alloc(from, to)` moves the storage and deallocates the source, so a result array is returned without duplication
**Allocatable locals are released at procedure exit**: An allocatable array declared inside a procedure is deallocated when the procedure returns, which is a scope-tied release the language provides

error.text: **There is no exception mechanism**: A failure is reported through a `stat=`/`iostat=` code or an `err=` label, and the caller has to test it
**A returned code can be ignored**: Nothing obliges a caller to look at `iostat`, so a failed `read`, `allocate`, or `deallocate` proceeds as though it had succeeded unless the program checks
**There is no composable result type**: No value carries either a result or an error, so error state travels in an extra out argument or in a saved flag

**`error stop` gives a defined abort**: Since Fortran 2008, `error stop` stops the program with a message or an integer stop-code, and Fortran 2018 added the optional `quiet=` specifier, so a fatal failure is stated rather than inferred from a negative status

**IEEE exceptional values are inspected through an intrinsic module**: `ieee_arithmetic` and `ieee_exceptions` let a program test `ieee_is_nan` and select a halting mode, but the checks are ordinary calls rather than a language guarantee
**A `pure` procedure cannot perform I/O**: An I/O failure is outside a `pure` procedure by construction, so a computational kernel has no I/O error channel to handle

concurrency.text: **Coarray images share memory by default**: A coarray declared with `codimension` is written by one image and read by another, and nothing in the language prevents the race
**Synchronisation is manual**: `sync all`, `sync images`, `event post`/`event wait`, and `lock`/`unlock` are image control statements the program must place at the right point

**`do concurrent` states an independent loop**: The construct asserts that the iterations have no interdependencies, and Fortran 2018 adds `local`, `local_init`, and `shared` locality specifications, so the compiler may parallelise it
**`atomic` and `critical` give a defined atomic access**: `atomic define`/`atomic_ref` and a `critical` construct express one update that must not interleave
**The practical parallel model sits outside the language**: Coarray support varies across compilers, so most high-performance code uses OpenMP directives or MPI calls

platform.text: **One standard source runs on every major compiler**: `gfortran`, `ifx`, `nagfor`, Cray, and LLVM `flang` accept standard-conforming Fortran on Linux, Windows, macOS, and the large HPC systems
**`iso_c_binding` names the interoperable interface**: `c_int`, `c_double`, `c_ptr`, and `c_funptr` let a Fortran routine be called from C and call C in return
**`iso_fortran_env` names the portable kinds and units**: `real64`, `int32`, and `input_unit` state a portable choice where `real(8)` names one machine's representation
**A compiled module is a binary interface**: A `module` is compiled to a file a consumer imports, so the interface is checked when the consumer is compiled
**Vendor directives are common in working code**: `!DIR$` and `!DEC$` directives, `REAL*8`, and `STRUCTURE`/`RECORD` appear in legacy HPC source, which binds it to one compiler

**Coarray support varies by compiler and platform**: A coarray program depends on the compiler's image implementation and its transport library, so its portability is weaker than that of a serial program

performance.text: **The program is compiled to machine code**: `gfortran`, `ifx`, and `flang` emit native objects for the target CPU, and the performance of an array kernel rivals C

**Array syntax maps onto the machine's loop nests**: `a = b + c` over whole arrays lets the compiler fuse and vectorise the loops, and `matmul` and `dot_product` have library or instruction implementations
**Nothing between the source and the CPU interprets**: A Fortran binary has no bytecode dispatch and no JIT warm-up
**The optimiser needs the aliasing facts**: Without `intent(in)`, `contiguous`, and `pure`, the compiler must assume a possible alias and cannot reorder the loops
**The floating-point contract is the compiler's flags**: `-O3` with `-ffast-math` or `-fp-model fast` changes the order of the operations, so the measured speed depends on the build options

ecosystem.text: **There is no standard package manager for the language**: Dependencies are resolved by a language-agnostic manager such as Spack or Conda or by the system manager, and the `fpm` package manager is young and small
**The numerical libraries are mature and standard**: BLAS, LAPACK, and the vendor-tuned kernels (MKL, ESSL) are callable from Fortran directly
**A compiler is available on every system**: A Fortran compiler is installed on every HPC cluster and is packaged for every common Linux distribution
**Interoperation with the C and Python ecosystems is standard**: `iso_c_binding` and the Python wrapper generators make a Fortran kernel callable from a Python array library
**Tooling beyond the compiler is thin**: Formatting, lint, and documentation come from small community projects (`fprettify`, `ford`) rather than from a supported toolchain
**The community is aging**: Adoption is declining and maintenance is concentrated in the HPC and numerical community

evolution.text: **The standard is backward compatible**: Fortran 90 source mostly compiles with a Fortran 2023 compiler, and only a small set of features has been deleted
**The compilers retain the deleted features as extensions**: `arithmetic IF` and `PAUSE`, both removed by the standard, are still accepted by the common compilers

**The intrinsic modules extend the language without editing it**: `iso_c_binding`, `iso_fortran_env`, and the parallel features were added as modules and new syntax rather than as changes to existing syntax
**A revision takes about a decade**: The editions are 2003, 2008, 2018, and 2023, so a needed feature waits years for the standard and lives as a compiler extension until then
**One program can hold several standards**: A single codebase can mix a Fortran 77 `common` block with a Fortran 2008 module, so the version in use is a property of the file
**An extension can become load-bearing**: A program that depends on a vendor directive cannot be moved to another compiler without an edit

domain.text: **Numerical and scientific computing is the design target**: Array syntax, complex arithmetic, real kinds, and the IEEE intrinsic modules fit it directly
**High-performance computing is the deepest adoption**: Weather, climate, and physics codes are written in Fortran, so the language dominates legacy HPC codebases
**`submodule` fits a large numerical codebase**: A module can declare the interface and a `submodule` hold the implementation, so changing a kernel recompiles only that submodule (Fortran 2008)
**Coarrays put a parallel program in the language**: A distributed-memory program is written without a call from a separate parallel library

**The language assumes a numerical, batch-shaped workload**: Text handling, dynamic data structures, and event-driven logic get little support, and the standard library is mainly the intrinsic procedures
**A new project often keeps Fortran for the kernel only**: The language is used where the inner loop must be native, and the orchestration moves to Python or C++

learning.text: **The core is small once `implicit none` is in place**: The statement forms, the intrinsic procedures, and the array expressions are a modest set
**The authoritative material is stable and complete**: The ISO standard, the compiler references, and *Modern Fortran Explained* cover the language in one place
**The array idiom has a direct mathematical reading**: A whole-array expression reads as the equation it computes
**Legacy syntax quirks create friction**: Fixed-form source with its column rules, implicit typing, and `common` blocks must be read to work on an existing codebase
**The array and parallel idioms take practice**: Array sections, `where`, and `do concurrent` read differently from an explicit loop, and the cost of a temporary array is easy to miss

syntax.text: **Fixed-form source is column-sensitive**: In a `.f` file a label sits in columns 1–5, a continuation mark in column 6, and a statement starts in column 7, so the layout carries meaning
**The language is verbose**: Kind, `intent`, and dimension accumulate on every dummy argument, and the internals of a procedure need their own `contains` block
**Whole-array expressions are compact**: `c = matmul(a, b) + alpha * c` states a matrix update in one line
**Free-form source is line-oriented and readable**: With `implicit none` and `use, only:`, a modern module reads close to the mathematics

**A `common` block's storage is positional**: Two declarations of the same block must list the fields in the same order with the same types, and the block's layout is a convention rather than a checked interface

testing.text: **`error stop` gives a test program a defined failure status**: A failing check stops the program with a non-zero status that a harness can read
**Run-time checks can be compiled in**: `-fcheck=all` (gfortran) and `-check all` (ifx) raise on an out-of-bounds subscript, an unassociated pointer, and a shape mismatch
**The numerical libraries ship their own test suites**: LAPACK and BLAS carry a published suite that exercises each routine, which is the numerical community's model
**There is no test framework in the language**: A test is a program that runs and compares, and a runner such as `pFUnit` or `test-drive` is a third-party library
**There is no assertion intrinsic**: A check is an explicit `if (cond) error stop`, so its presence is a written decision
**The result depends on the flags and the hardware**: The summation order, `-ffast-math`, and the fused multiply-add change the last bits, so a test must fix the build and compare with a tolerance

security.text: **Memory safety depends on a checked build**: An out-of-bounds subscript, an unassociated pointer, and a mismatch between an actual and a dummy argument are found only when the compiler is asked to check them, and the standard requires no run-time check
**There is no dynamic evaluation of source text**: The language has no `eval`, no reflective call by name, and no string-to-code path, so a value cannot become code
**`intent(in)` prevents a write through the callee**: The compiler refuses an assignment to an `intent(in)` dummy argument, so the read-only direction is enforced
**The C interface hands safety to the neighbour**: `c_ptr` and `type(c_funptr)` are raw addresses, and the guarantees of the C code on the other side become part of the program
**There is no capability model and no sandbox**: A program runs with the authority of the process, and the mitigations come from the operating system and the linker
**A `pure` procedure cannot corrupt state through I/O or a global**: The effect set of a `pure` procedure is empty by construction

tradeoffs: **`implicit none` is the modern practice, not the standard default**: A project chooses to require it, and the language permits implicit typing for the old source
**Column-major order is a deliberate numerical choice**: Array expressions follow Fortran's storage order, which is what the linear-algebra kernels are written for
**The aliasing rules are what the optimiser needs**: The standard's restrictions let the compiler vectorise a loop, which costs flexibility and buys speed
**`goto` remains for compatibility**: It is retained so that decades of code keeps compiling, and a new program need not use it
**Whole-array syntax exists so the compiler chooses the loop nest**: The programmer gives up per-loop control in exchange for vectorisation
**The legacy corpus is working, tested numerical code**: The aging ecosystem holds decades of validated physics and linear-algebra routines
verdict: Fortran's design produces a low core score, because the constructs that make the numerical work fast are the constructs that couple. Array expressions and `pure` procedures are real separations, and a module with a `submodule` separates an interface from its implementation. But implicit typing hides a misspelled variable, `common` blocks and module variables are global mutable state, a `pointer` is freed by hand with no owner, and an error is a code the caller may ignore. Main strengths: the fit to numerical computing is exact, array performance rivals C, and one standard source runs on every major compiler. Main weaknesses: the ecosystem is small and aging, the revision cycle is slow, and the syntax of a legacy file depends on column positions.

ai-readiness.text: Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [@joel2025lowresource].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.
